about.title: Redwood City Product Liability Claims
about.longDescription: A faulty product rarely gives warning. It might be a lithium battery that overheats in a Redwood City apartment, a child's car seat that fails during a collision on Woodside Road, or a power tool bought along El Camino Real that comes apart mid-use. When something you relied on causes harm here in San Mateo County, California law offers a route many people do not expect: strict liability. In plain terms, you generally do not have to prove the manufacturer was careless. You need to show the product had a defect — in its design, in how that particular unit was made, or in the warnings that came with it — and that the defect caused your injury. Responsibility can stretch across several companies. The maker, the distributor and the local retailer that sold it may each be answerable. LawProactive is not a law firm. We are a free service that puts Redwood City residents in touch with an independent attorney who takes these cases on contingency. Hold onto the product, its packaging and any receipts, and reach out when you are ready.

items.question: Do I have to prove the company was careless to win a product liability claim in California?
items.answer: Usually not. California applies strict liability to most defective product cases, so the central questions are whether the product had a design, manufacturing or warning defect and whether that defect caused your injury. Negligence can still be argued in some cases, but it is not the only path. An attorney can explain which theory fits your situation.

items.question: I was injured in a crash on US-101 near Redwood City and suspect an airbag or tire failed. Is that a product liability case?
items.answer: It can be. Redwood City recorded 305 injury collisions in 2025, and some crashes involve a vehicle component that did not perform as designed. If a defective airbag, tire, seatbelt or other part contributed to your injuries, the manufacturer or supplier of that part may be liable in addition to any driver at fault. Keep the vehicle from being repaired or scrapped until an attorney has reviewed it.

items.question: What should I do with the product that hurt me?
items.answer: Keep it, and keep it as close to its post-incident condition as possible. Do not try to fix it, return it to the store, or throw away the packaging, manuals or receipt. Photographs of the item and your injuries help too. The attorney you are connected with will want to examine the product, and it is often the key to establishing the defect.
